content: Banandine is a fictional psychoactive substance that is claimed to be derived from banana peels. The original recipe for extracting this substance was published as a hoax in the Berkeley Barb in March 1967. The concept gained further attention when William Powell, believing the hoax to be true, included the method in his 1970 book The Anarchist Cookbook under the name Musa Sapientum Banandine, referencing the scientific name of the banana. However, researchers at New York University have confirmed that banana peels do not contain any intoxicating chemicals, and smoking them only produces a placebo effect. Despite this, the idea of Banandine has persisted as a popular urban legend over the years. Banana peels do contain significant amounts of the non-psychoactive neurotransmitters tyramine and dopamine. These chemicals can affect individuals taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), as they are present in many foods at higher concentrations. People using MAOIs are advised to avoid such substances due to the risk of severe interactions. The most notable effect of this interaction is a dangerous spike in blood pressure, potentially leading to a hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias, or even death. Additionally, bananas contain tryptophan, which, when ingested, increases serotonin levels in the body. A study by Xiao et al. in 1998 demonstrated that consuming two bananas daily for three days raised blood serotonin levels by 16%. However, it remains uncertain whether smoking tryptophan would be an effective method of administration. The myth of Banandine has also permeated popular culture. Donovan's hit single Mellow Yellow, released in the same month as the Berkeley Barb hoax, was mistakenly believed to be the origin of the myth for years. In an October 2005 interview on NPR's Fresh Air, Donovan clarified that the rumor was actually started by folk singer Country Joe McDonald in San Francisco, a week before the release of Mellow Yellow. McDonald has corroborated this story, adding that the rumor led to a banana shortage in Berkeley as concert-goers bought up all available bananas for experimentation. The myth resurfaced in the late 1980s when the satirical punk band The Dead Milkmen released a song about the effects of smoking banana peels. Even the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) investigated the claims. The British band The Prodigy referenced the myth in the inner sleeve of their debut album Experience, where member Leeroy Thornhill jokingly invited people to smoke banana skins. Similarly, Ray Stevens' song Thirty-Five Year Old Hippie Class Reunion alludes to the hoax, humorously escalating to a suggestion of smoking the entire contents of a pet store by the song's conclusion.
